title: What Is a Ring Tree in Pay Per Call?
h1: What is a ring tree in pay per call?
description: A ring tree (or ping tree) routes each inbound call to a sequence of buyers until one accepts it. Here is how ring trees work and when to use one.
faq: What is the difference between a ring tree and a ping tree?

They describe the same idea. "Ping tree" comes from form-lead routing, where a lead is pinged to buyers in turn; "ring tree" is the phone-call version, where an inbound call is offered to buyers until one accepts and the call connects.
Is a ring tree the same as real-time bidding?

Not quite. A ring tree is the structure that offers a call to buyers in some order; real-time bidding is one way to decide that order, by price. You can run a ring tree by fixed priority, by bid, or a mix of both. See how real-time call bidding works.
Why use a ring tree instead of one buyer?

Because a single buyer who is closed, capped or simply not interested means a lost call. A ring tree offers the call to the next buyer instead, so more calls connect and each one has a chance to sell for what it is worth.
body:
A ring tree is a way of routing an inbound phone call to several buyers in turn until one of them accepts it. The name comes from the shape: one call enters at the top and branches out to buyer after buyer until it finds a home. If you have heard the term ping tree for form leads, a ring tree is the same idea applied to live calls. It is the backbone of how networks sell a single call to the right buyer in real time.

How a ring tree works

  1. A call comes in on a tracking number tied to a campaign.
  2. Filters run first. Blocked numbers, repeat callers, opening hours, state rules and daily caps decide which buyers are even eligible.
  3. The call is offered to buyers in order. That order can be a fixed priority list, or set by who bids the most for the call.
  4. The first buyer who accepts wins. The call connects to them and the price is recorded.
  5. If no one accepts, the call falls back to a voicemail, another campaign, or a message — so the caller is not simply dropped.

Ring tree, waterfall and real-time bidding

These terms overlap, so it helps to separate them. A waterfall is a ring tree ordered by fixed priority: buyer A, then B, then C. Real-time bidding is a ring tree ordered by price: the call goes to the highest bid above your floor. Most platforms let you combine them — for example, run an auction first, then fall back to a priority waterfall if nobody bids. Our guide to how real-time call bidding works covers the auction side in detail.

Why ring trees matter

  • Higher fill rate — a capped or closed buyer no longer costs you the call; it moves on to the next.
  • Better payout per call — when order is set by bid, each call tends to sell for closer to its true value.
  • Fewer wasted callers — a sensible fall-back means even an unsold call ends in voicemail or a message, not silence.

Setting up a ring tree that behaves

Three settings do most of the work. The order (priority, bid or both) decides who hears the call first. The timeout on each step keeps the caller from waiting too long before the call moves on. And the fall-back decides what happens when nobody takes the call. Get those right and the ring tree runs quietly in the background while callers connect.
